Experiments on two independently fabricated 72-unit silicon processors show that a nominally identical device cannot reproduce the target's responses even after its passive phase profile is fully compensated. Combining isotropic routing with spectral readout yields 1107 bits per challenge, exceeding previous results by two orders of magnitude, with 49.8% inter-challenge and 50.0% inter-chip Hamming distances and a 4.9% intra-chip distance. These results establish general-purpose programmable photonic processors as reconfigurable, high-capacity hardware roots of trust.

title: Exceptional unidirectional radiation modes
abstract: Singularities such as exceptional points (EPs) and bound states in the continuum (BICs) fundamentally reshape the spectral response of non-Hermitian open systems, unlocking exotic physical phenomena and unprecedented ways of wave manipulation. Nevertheless, the radiation behaviors of modes evolving around these singularities lack a unified picture. Here we show that a mode originating from a BIC can radiate unidirectionally, exhibiting a quality factor that continuously varies in parameter space from a near-infinite value (near the BIC) to a finite lower bound as it coalesces with the other (leaky) mode at an EP. The crossing of the unidirectional radiation mode and the EP in parameter space results in not only merged poles (resonant EP) but also merged zeros (absorbing EP) of the scattering matrix, along with a counterintuitive reversal of radiation direction decoupled from the coalesced eigenmodes under near-field excitation. These phenomena are experimentally observed in an acoustic waveguide system featuring two side-branch resonant cavities with deliberate frequency detuning and asymmetric dissipation. Our findings reveal the intrinsic connection between eigenmode topology and radiation behavior in open systems, offering a viable route for tailoring scattering and radiation responses via non-Hermitian modulations.

title: A Symmetry-Stratified Framework for Phase Transitions: Thermodynamic States, Critical Dynamics, and Spectral Mechanical Signatures
abstract: Structural symmetry, thermodynamic phase stability, and elastic-wave response provide related but distinct descriptions of a transforming solid. We formulate a symmetry-stratified framework that connects these descriptions through a finite-dimensional internal state and a parent-invariant free energy. Stabilizers classify structural states, whereas free-energy comparisons and stability conditions determine equilibrium branches and dissipative evolution. Equivariance ensures that the frozen elastic tangent inherits the structural stabilizer. Equality requires additional identifiability conditions. Little-group representations and degenerate perturbation theory then determine whether an acoustic doublet splits and the first nonzero splitting order $p$. On a selected continuous branch with order-parameter exponent $β$, a regular, observable acoustic gap scales as $|t|^{pβ}$, provided critical self-energies and structural relaxation do not dominate the measurement. Explicit tensorial and cubic-to-tetragonal realizations yield linear and quadratic splitting channels, together with directionally protected degeneracies. Separate numerical benchmarks examine free-energy reconstruction, coexistence, elastic compatibility, finite-temperature spectra, and controlled critical readouts. Reanalysis of NiTi measurements illustrates effective elastic degeneracy, thermal-history dependence, and the predictive value of independently measured phase fractions. Most importantly, the framework identifies the constitutive and measurement assumptions required to infer structural changes from mechanical spectra.

title: Geometric control of diffusive relaxation: spectral design, transport bounds and transverse mode isolation
abstract: Geometric confinement changes both thermal relaxation and heat throughput, but these effects need not be governed by the same conduction path. We establish a distinction between serial and parallel geometries for passive, homogeneous Fourier conductors at fixed material properties, volume and length. For a reduced variable-area conductor, two logarithmic shape harmonics independently tune two selected Bloch-rate pairs, and exact local transport level sets permit spectral redistribution at fixed effective diffusivity. A nonperturbative weighted Poincaré bound, however, requires the effective axial diffusivity to vanish if the first positive insulated rate tends to zero at fixed length. This obstruction is avoided by continuous parallel paths with weak transverse exchange. Capacity-weighted networks identify the exchange mechanism, and a three-dimensional product domain provides an exact bulk realization. Its axial conductance remains $κV/L^2$, while exactly one positive insulated rate vanishes and the next approaches a positive limit set by axial, chamber and neck diffusion. The slow rate is asymptotically the transverse neck conductance times the sum of inverse chamber capacities. Spectral projection estimates translate this separation into a preparation- and readout-dependent observation window. The result is metastable retention of a temperature contrast under insulated conditions, not a second equilibrium state. It identifies when geometrical control of internal equilibration can be separated from macroscopic heat transport.

title: Colloquium: Isotopes for medicine and fundamental physics
abstract: Isotopes, variants of elements distinguished by their neutron number, have important applications for medicine and fundamental science. This review explores the historical challenges and new technologies for enriching and detecting isotopes. We motivate the work by challenges posed by three of history's greatest scientists: James Clerk Maxwell's thought experiment on thermodynamics, Ernest Rutherford's practical dilemma in radiochemistry, and Albert Einstein's questions about the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. The journey to meet these challenges has catalyzed the development of innovative techniques for isotope separation. These advancements can mitigate the worldwide crisis in the supply of enriched isotopes. We then explore the expected impact of these new technologies on medicine, which include radioisotopes for cancer therapy and stable isotopes as tracers for metabolism. We explain the importance of developing scalable techniques for isotope detection and how it can help with early detection of certain diseases. Finally, we turn to basic science, outlining proposed new tests of quantum mechanics that utilize radioactive atomic clocks to probe the fundamental nature of determinism and distinguishability of atoms.

title: Design and Modeling of Graded Base III-Nitride HBTs for High-Frequency Applications
abstract: This work analyzes the high-frequency performance constraints of AlGaN/GaN heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) and proposes a novel band-engineered graded base N-polar AlGaN/GaN HBT and evaluates the RF performances. Unlike conventional p-GaN base designs, we propose a graded base in the N-polar orientation which offers polarization-induced hole accumulation with quasi-electric field-assisted minority carrier transport. The proposed design simultaneously mitigates the longstanding current crowding, Webster effect, and conventional base resistance limitations. Using well-calibrated two-dimensional TCAD simulations, the proposed compositionally graded base HBT projects peak f_T/f_{MAX} of 190/200 GHz with a power density (V_{BR}I_{MAX}/8 > 20 W/mm), offering a promising pathway toward simultaneous high-frequency and high-power GaN millimeter-wave electronics.

title: Generation of neutron Bessel beams
abstract: Matter waves can exhibit structured wavefields analogous to those of light, offering new means of controlling the spatial and angular-momentum degrees of freedom of massive particles. Bessel beams are a fundamental class of structured waves that exhibit non-diffracting propagation, self-healing, and well-defined orbital angular momentum (OAM). Here, we experimentally realize neutron Bessel beams by imprinting a nanoscale conical phase gradient onto a neutron wavefront. By incorporating azimuthal phase gradients, we generate zeroth-, third-, and sixth-order Bessel beams, demonstrating direct control of both the OAM and radial structure of a massive particle. We also propose a neutron Bessel-grating interferometer, complementary to established optical and electron interferometric methods, in which varying the radial grating period by approximately 100 nm yields a controlled Gouy phase shift of $π$. These results establish neutron Bessel beams as a new platform for diffractive neutron focusing and provide an experimental foundation for theoretical studies of Bessel beams in neutron scattering, decay, and OAM characterization.

title: Local orbital magnetization and Chern markers from equilibrium local currents
abstract: Local currents carry the orbital magnetization of a macroscopic sample and are key for modeling inhomogeneous magnetic materials and for understanding magnetoelectric and topological responses. However, producing realistic simulated images of local currents in inhomogeneous systems remains challenging. Building upon recent work on stochastic estimation methods for tight-binding models, we show that all matrix elements of positive semidefinite operators defined on a lattice can be obtained at once from a single set of filtered random vectors. This eliminates the need for independent simulations previously required for off-diagonal elements, which significantly speeds up the calculation of spatial maps of local currents. Further, we express bond currents in terms of loop currents that obey a discrete Poisson equation, with the current vorticity acting as the source term. Its solution yields a local orbital magnetization. In analogy with the global Středa relation, the derivative of this magnetization with respect to the chemical potential defines a new local Chern marker. Built entirely from bond currents, it requires no position operator and is not bound by the zero-sum rule of projector markers in open samples. Hence, it is free of boundary-compensation artifacts, and its sample average converges to the bulk Chern number in a controlled fashion.

title: Magnon high-harmonic generation by nonlinearities of spin torque driven by phonon-mediated crossing of many-body energy levels of bright and dark excitons
abstract: Recent intense experimental focus on CrSBr, a two-dimensional (2D) antiferromagnetic semiconductor, has revealed numerous surprises in its response to ultrafast optical drive. We demonstrate that a single microscopic mechanism accounts for two of them---high-harmonic generation of magnons and persistence of magnon oscillations over \mbox{$\sim 1$ ns} time scale that is much longer than the femtosecond laser pulse (fsLP) pump duration. This mechanism arises from an unusually complex interplay of four different fundamental quasiparticles of condensed matter physics: magnons, optically bright and dark excitons, and phonons. By viewing magnons as the system and the other three quasiparticles as a quantum many-body bath, we derive an extended Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (eLLG) equation. Its new term generated by the bath is spatially nonlocal and time-dependent, as well as strongly {\em nonlinear} when the {\em crossing of many-body energy levels} of bright and dark excitons occurs via phonon mediation. It also resembles the so-called field-like spin-transfer torque (STT) in spintronics, but STT is driven there with current pulses, so it explains the microscopic origin of the recently experimentally conjectured {\em excitonic STT}. Since dark excitons supply energy to magnons long after the fsLP is switched off, such a reservoir opens avenues for its engineering and applications in optospintronics and optomagnonics, neuromorphic computing, and quantum transduction.

title: Emergent Orbital Hall Currents in Disordered and Amorphous Materials
abstract: The role of disorder in orbital transport remains a central open question in orbitronics. Using a real-space formulation of itinerant orbital angular momentum, we investigate the real-time or- bital Hall transport in single-orbital square-lattice and graphene-based systems. We demonstrate that both structural (polycrystalline and amorphous) and electrostatic disorder can generate siz- able orbital Hall currents that are absent in their pristine counterparts. Remarkably, in amorphous graphene, these currents persist over extended timescales and across a broad energy window around charge neutrality, despite the strong localization of electronic states. Consistent with recent exper- imental evidence, our findings establish amorphous quantum materials as promising platforms for disorder-engineered orbitronic functionality.

title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
abstract: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts. Most of the configurations we tested become more accurate than a reference with relaxation and dephasing disabled, most strongly at $T_2=1\,μ$s, where total memory capacity drops, and still at $T_2=5$-$10\,μ$s, where memory is only redistributed across delays. For autonomous generation, we train the readout with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation to expose it to states reached under its own feedback. We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble. For chaotic forecasting, in contrast, prediction horizons at $T_2=1\,μ$s shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations relative to that reference. For the noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor, the model produces a smooth, approximately closed orbit, and neither captures the target's scatter nor follows its trajectory pointwise. We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.

title: Spectral localizers in phase space: $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariants for higher-order, semimetal, and valley modes
abstract: Topologically protected gapless modes emerge across multiple platforms, ranging from nodes in the band structure to boundary states in topologically non-trivial insulators, with each case governed by distinct topological classifications and invariants. Here, we generalize the spectral localizer method to establish a unified framework for topological gapless modes. The spectral localizer reduces the original Hamiltonian to a zero-dimensional operator by recursively applying quantum confining operators, which need not be diagonal in either position or momentum space, as previously assumed. In phase space, the zero-manifold of the semiclassical confining operators forms a shell enclosing the gapless mode of interest, analogous to the Teo-Kane framework for topological defects. The localizer yields a zero-dimensional invariant, such as a signature, a determinant sign, or a Pfaffian sign, capturing both $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ classifications. This single construction thus encompasses diverse scenarios, including hinge modes in higher-order topological insulators, individual Dirac nodes in semimetals, and valley-selective topological boundary modes. We illustrate our approach using lattice models in symmetry classes A, AIII, AII, and D, verifying that topological transitions coincide with a vanishing gap in the spectral localizer operator.

title: Investigating Thermal Boundary Conductance in Monolayer Transition Metal Dichalcogenides: A Systematic Comparison of Advanced Nanoscale Thermometry Techniques
abstract: Thermal boundary conductance (TBC) plays a crucial role in heat dissipation in two-dimensional (2D) devices. However, reported values for 2D material classes such as monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) can vary by more than an order of magnitude across the literature, making it difficult to determine whether these differences come from the materials themselves or from the measurement methods used. To address this issue, this article presents a systematic, cross-technique study of the interfacial heat transport in four TMD monolayers supported on a sapphire substrate, using three of the most representative methods: Raman thermometry, scanning thermal microscopy (SThM) and frequency domain thermoreflectance (FDTR). By conducting all measurements on the same sets of samples, the influence of sample-to-sample variation is minimized allowing for a direct comparison of the three approaches. The results reveal a variation in the measured values depending on both the material and the measurement technique. By directly comparing these results we can elucidate on the origin of the differences and underpin sources of uncertainty in each of the characterisation methods. Taken together, these results provide a direct experimental benchmark for studies of 2D material interfaces and offer practical guidance for the selection and interpretation of thermal metrology.

title: A Tutorial on Complementarity-Based Contact Models for Robotics
abstract: Simulating rigid-body dynamics with contact is fundamental to robotics, from motion synthesis and control to mechanism design. Many widely used simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations, whose physical assumptions and numerical solution require substantial background. While excellent surveys, monographs, and course notes exist, they mostly address computational mechanics or computer graphics or document a single simulator. To the best of our knowledge, a self-contained pedagogical treatment for robotics, bringing these formulations and their solvers together with complete derivations and a unified notation, does not yet exist. This tutorial addresses this gap by connecting rigid-body dynamics, conic optimization, and frictional contact. In particular, we explain how complementarity conditions encode non-penetration and frictional dissipation, determining separation, sticking, and sliding without prescribed contact modes. We distinguish equivalent transcriptions from convex relaxations, showing how the latter can introduce artifacts such as lift-off and creep. We examine the existence and uniqueness of motion and contact forces, including the solver's role in selecting among multiple solutions. We then compare first-order and Newton-based methods, explain regularization and proximal strategies, and discuss trade-offs between computational cost, robustness, and physical fidelity. Connections to widely used simulators, optimal control, and differentiable simulation help readers interpret simulation results, choose suitable formulations and solvers, and develop their own contact dynamics routines.

title: PhyDEX: A Benchmark for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language-Action Models via Dynamic Extrinsic Dexterity
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper--object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3\%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.

title: Learning Control-Relevant Koopman Representations from Input-Output Trajectories
abstract: Predictive accuracy alone does not ensure that data-driven Koopman representations are suitable for output-feedback control. This paper develops a continuous-time framework for learning control-relevant Koopman representations using only measured input-output trajectories. A causal encoder constructs the lifted state from a finite input-output window, and an additive lifted model is identified by integral regression. We distinguish observability, input-map compatibility, controllability, and data informativity. We characterize compatibility with a constant lifted input matrix, quantify input-map mismatch, and, under exact lifting assumptions, relate iterated Lie brackets to the controllable subspace of the lifted realization. A covariance-normalized finite-horizon observability criterion is optimized subject to separate bounds on output-prediction and temporal-consistency errors. Under the stated exactness and observability assumptions, the encoded lifted state depends only on the current nonlinear state. For approximate representations, we bound the difference between encodings of distinct past trajectories ending at the same state. An exactly liftable controlled system provides analytical ground truth, while a controlled Duffing oscillator illustrates the approximate setting, for which an informative exact additive lifting on an open set is shown to be impossible. On the exact benchmark, encoder initialization determines whether the learned representation recovers the analytical lift. In the reported Duffing experiments, observability promotion improves nominal Gramian measures without improving observer-based estimation or tracking, while updating the lifted-state estimate through the encoder at every sampling instant has a larger effect on tracking accuracy.

title: From power to spectrum: an off-the-shelf photodiode turned into a spectrometer by its bias alone
abstract: Computational spectrometers replace dispersive optics with detectors whose spectral response can be varied, but every reported single-detector device obtains this response through dedicated fabrication: two-dimensional heterostructures, graded epitaxial junctions, organic stacks, filters or photonic circuits. We demonstrate a generic, fabrication-free alternative in which a standard commercial photodiode becomes a spectrometer through its electrical drive alone, requiring no modification of the device, no optical filter and no modulation of the light. The mechanism is bias-modulated optoelectronic chromatic dispersion (OED): light of different wavelengths is absorbed at different depths, and a sinusoidal bias changes how carriers generated at each depth are collected, so that every spectrum is encoded in the shape of the photocurrent waveform over one bias period. Applied to an unmodified InGaAs PIN photodiode at room temperature, a 10 us waveform decoded by a neural network reconstructs spectra of one to three laser lines across the 80 nm of the telecom C+L band, locating the lines to 0.3-0.4 nm, counting them in about 99% of measurements and identifying their power levels, with line shifts tracked to tens of picometres. Because OED relies on universal semiconductor transport physics, the approach is material-agnostic and applies in principle to any off-the-shelf photodiode, turning detectors already deployed as power monitors into low-cost spectral sensors.

title: Thermal-Guided Ensemble Reinforcement Learning for Regime-Adaptive Short-Term GPU Power Forecasting in AI Data Centers
abstract: AI data centers (AIDCs) introduce bursty and regime-dependent load patterns, posing significant challenges for reliable energy management and predictive grid control. To address these challenges, this letter proposes a thermal-guided ensemble reinforcement learning framework for probabilistic AIDC load forecasting. A soft actor-critic (SAC) agent with a simplex-preserving policy adaptively weights LSTM, TCN, and Transformer predictors at every time step based on their realized errors. A thermal-guided neural correction estimates the ensemble residual, while a sensitivity-projection regularizer enforces the non-negative sensitivity of power to GPU utilization and temperature. The corrected ensemble output is further processed by a Bayesian probabilistic layer to produce predictive distributions and quantify forecasting uncertainty. Case studies on 1-second MIT Supercloud telemetry show that the proposed method reduces the normalized mean absolute error to about 1% across all computing regimes, compared with 4-11% for deep learning-based and ensemble learning benchmarks, and converges faster with narrower prediction intervals than a DRL ensemble without thermal guidance.

title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
abstract: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.

title: An Open-Source ROS 2 Framework for Shared Control in Surgical Teleoperation: Integrating the Haply Inverse3 with the da Vinci Research Kit
abstract: Surgical teleoperation deprives surgeons of touch, forcing visual inference of tissue forces; the commercial platforms now restoring force feedback remain closed, preventing open research on haptic shared control. This paper provides a system contribution: it presents an open-source, ROS 2-native framework that integrates the compact, three-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) Haply Inverse3 haptic device with the da~Vinci Research Kit (dVRK). The framework includes a novel mapping strategy that combines 3-DOF translational device input with separately tracked VerseGrip orientation into 6-DOF patient-side manipulator commands. Two virtual-fixture-inspired guidance modes serve as reference implementations to evaluate the framework in a within-subjects user study on a teleoperated hot-wire benchmark task in simulation, and the architecture is further demonstrated on physical dVRK hardware. Relative to unassisted manual control, linear guidance significantly reduced both the number of wire contacts and the task completion time, whereas the progressive-stiffness guidance produced consistent but statistically non-significant trends in the same direction. Subjective ratings of workload, agency, and satisfaction showed favorable descriptive trends for the guidance modes. The results demonstrate the feasibility of haptic shared control with a compact device coupled to the dVRK and provide an openly available, reproducible platform for future research. They further suggest that simpler linear feedback may be more robust for inexperienced operators than more complex profiles.

title: Optimal Scheduling of Multi-Site AI Data Centers in Day-Ahead Markets
abstract: AI data centers are among the fastest-growing loads on the power grid, and their flexibility is increasingly sought by grid operators. Using it requires a model that links what an operator controls, namely GPU power caps, job timing and job placement, to the power drawn at each site and the electricity prices it faces. This paper develops such a framework for a multi-site AI data-center fleet. It represents GPU power-cap levels; deferrable jobs with deadlines and inference with response-time headroom; and site facility power, and casts the fleet schedule as a linear program solved on day-ahead prices. A year-long simulation on 2025 California Independent System Operator (CAISO) day-ahead prices in three data-center markets demonstrates the framework. Coordinated scheduling lowers the fleet's energy cost by 6.3% at equal work. Four operating modes, each adding one capability, split this saving into efficient GPU operation that needs no price signal, price response in time, and routing work between sites.

title: Optimal Control in Pairs Trading with Negative-Power Utility
abstract: We solve a finite-horizon consumption and investment problem in a pairs trading model with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck spread and utility $U(x)=-x^{-γ}$, $γ>0$. Linearizing the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation gives explicit formulas for the value function and the optimal feedback control. A budget inequality and concavity verify optimality over all admissible strategies with nonnegative wealth on every finite horizon, without Novikov's condition. Under the optimal feedback, wealth and consumption admit deterministic upper bounds when the interest rate $r$ is at most the mean-reversion rate $κ$. If $r>κ$, each exceeds any prescribed level with positive probability at every time after the start. If $r>\sqrt{2+γ} κ$, there is an explicit critical horizon at and beyond which expected terminal wealth is infinite, while optimal expected utility is finite. When the critical time falls before maturity, expected wealth at that time is finite exactly when the initial spread is zero. We also show that the suprema of the negative powers of optimal wealth and consumption are integrable on every finite horizon exactly for orders $0<m\le 1+γ$.

title: Minimization of free energy in a Poisson--Boltzmann problem
abstract: In this paper, we study a mathematical model in which an ionic solution composed of several types of spherical ions is confined between two uniformly charged parallel planes. The ion concentrations at equilibrium, determined by the interplay between thermal and electrostatic effects, are obtained by minimizing the free energy of the system. The resulting minimization problem is infinite-dimensional, and we prove the existence and uniqueness of its solution by means of a norm-convergence direct method based on the Banach--Saks property of the space in which the problem is posed. The existence proof is technically challenging because the functional to be minimized is not coercive in general. Three illustrative problems are considered and solved numerically.

title: Local velocimetry for atomic superfluids: from Riemann rarefaction waves to quantized vortices
abstract: We demonstrate local velocimetry for atomic superfluids in two dimensions (2D). Using matter-wave interferometry based on Raman--Bragg beam splitters, we map the local gradient of the phase of the superfluid's wavefunction onto displacement of the interference fringes and reconstruct the 2D velocity field. We illustrate the capabilities of this technique by applying it to two canonical problems. First, we directly observe the self-similar evolution of the velocity field in 1D Riemann rarefaction flows. Second, we map out the full 2D velocity field around quantized vortices, explicitly demonstrating the quantization of velocity circulation.

title: Activity-driven motion and deformation of a circular membrane domain
abstract: Lipid bilayer membranes are nanometer-thin fluid interfaces characterized by both in-plane fluidity and lateral compositional heterogeneity. Cholesterol-rich liquid domains ("lipid rafts") are thought to regulate the spatial organization of membrane proteins and numerous cellular processes. While the passive diffusion and equilibrium shape fluctuations of membrane domains are well understood, much less is known about how the activity of molecular machines, such as protein pumps and enzymes, influences their mobility and deformation. Here, we analyze the dynamics of a membrane domain driven by an embedded molecular machine within the framework of two-dimensional Stokes flow. The molecular machine is modeled as a point singularity of the two-dimensional Stokes equations, including both rotational and irrotational singularities corresponding to force and source multipoles. We show that, despite being force-free, both force and source dipoles generate active flows that propel the membrane domain. For a force dipole undergoing rotational diffusion, the domain motion is diffusive at long times but exhibits a transient superdiffusive regime at intermediate times.

title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors
abstract: Neutron stars provide a natural laboratory for superfluid matter under extreme conditions. Its nonlinear dynamics is central to pulsar glitches, their possible links to fast radio bursts, and tidal interactions in inspiralling binaries. We develop a general-relativistic superfluid hydrodynamics framework incorporating entrainment, vortex forces, and line energy, and derive, for the first time, necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity. We also show that commonly used dissipative, force-balanced formulations without line tension are generically ill-posed at short wavelengths because of the Donnelly-Glaberson instability. Exploiting the analogy between vortex arrays with tension and force-free electrodynamics, we recast vortex dynamics in terms of effective electric and magnetic fields and drift velocities. This motivates a new finite-volume scheme combining constrained transport of superfluid vorticity with implicit electric-field evolution, enabling stable numerical evolution of the full system. We validate the scheme using an exact solution to the relativistic superfluid Riemann problem and Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, among other tests. Finally, we simulate dynamical, global general-relativistic two-fluid neutron-star equilibria, validate their oscillation modes, and present the first simplified calculation of superfluid interior spin-down with prescribed vortex release and repinning. The resulting stationary state retains both a net twist in the vortex array and residual differential rotation of the superfluid. Our framework thus enables nonlinear numerical studies of general-relativistic superfluid dynamics in neutron-star interiors.

title: Lagrangian transport driven by travelling waves in a radially deforming circular cavity
abstract: A travelling deformation of a circular cavity wall can carry particles with the wave or against it. For two counter-propagating waves of azimuthal order $m$ and amplitudes $a$ and $b$, the leading axisymmetric component of the total (Lagrangian) drift scales with the intensity difference $S_3=|a|^2-|b|^2$. We obtain the radial profile of the azimuthal drift in closed form in the viscous limit, where the Womersley number $\mathrm{Wo}$ tends to zero, and by quadrature for any finite $\mathrm{Wo}>0$. The total drift is the sum of the Eulerian mean velocity and the Stokes drift. For radial wall motion with $m\ge2$ and unequal wave intensities, the total drift follows the stronger of the two waves throughout the interior in the viscous limit, although the Stokes drift changes sign with radius for all $\mathrm{Wo}$. For $m=2$ and large $\mathrm{Wo}$, the predicted total drift just inside a radially moving wall opposes the wave to leading order in wall amplitude. For the same travelling shape, the total drift there follows the wave when the wall material also moves tangentially to preserve local arc length to first order. For the radial wall at large $\mathrm{Wo}$, the near-wall profile consists of the planar Longuet-Higgins result and a closed-form curvature correction. At large $m$ the core rotation approaches Tuck's finite-Reynolds-number waving-sheet result. At $m=2$ and $\mathrm{Wo}^2=10$, moving-domain simulations recover the leading-order drift coefficients for both wall motions.

title: Flux-induced condensation in a radial geometry
abstract: Stirring and shear usually suppress phase separation, but transport through a boundary can induce it. We study a binary mixture that is stable everywhere at rest and fills a two-dimensional annulus. The inner boundary is semipermeable and exchanges material with a permeate held at a fixed chemical potential, so that a steady flux of one component crosses the annulus. Although this driven system carries a steady current and produces entropy, within Model B dynamics its steady state is an equilibrium profile in an effective external field that is logarithmic in the distance from the center. Its strength is not imposed from outside but set by the permeate and the permeability of the boundary. Above a threshold driving flux, a condensed annulus forms around the inner boundary. It is bounded by a stationary front whose radius depends exponentially on the ratio of the bulk driving force to the flux. The front is pinned by the effective field and does not coarsen, and the threshold flux decreases only as the inverse logarithm of the system size. The driving flux shifts the phase lines but leaves the critical temperature unchanged. Interfacial tension gives rise to a critical nucleus and to a fold, at which the condensed state ceases to exist, with a threshold that we obtain in closed form. Numerical solutions confirm these predictions and reveal a hysteresis loop bounded by two saddle-node bifurcations. By symmetry, the theory also describes cavitation around a sink.

title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
abstract: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

title: Process-Knowledge-Guided Latent Diffusion for Generative Design of Porous Architectures: A Case Study in Aerosol Jet Printing
abstract: Printed porous layouts interleave functional material with open channels, and the layout that uses the material best depends on how the process settings shape the deposit. Generative models propose layouts quickly, but a generator that does not receive the process setting samples from the same distribution at every setting, even when the process-dependent score ranks candidate layouts differently. This paper examines whether process knowledge can steer a latent diffusion generator toward layouts suited to a given process setting in a prescribed design domain. We formulate a process-dependent utilization score in which a process model sets the length over which the utility of printed material decays with distance from a channel. The generator combines a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent representation, a topology U-Net, a ControlNet domain branch, and a separately trained regressor that predicts the score from noised latents; the domain branch conditions each denoising step and the regressor gradient steers it. The method is applied to aerosol jet printing, where the atomizer and sheath gas flows enter the score through the flow-focusing relation. Across seven modeled flow settings, the lowest-scoring candidate layout of a domain differed between settings in 191 of 500 domains. In a sampling study, the mean directly computed score on three validation domains and one test domain was 0.642 with domain conditioning alone, 0.636 at a weight of 300, and 0.450 at 12,000 (112 scores per weight; lower is better). The results support process-knowledge-guided generation as an approach to process-specific porous design under the stated assumptions.

title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
abstract: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

title: Beyond corridor averages: Lane-level validation of microscopic freeway simulation with empirically parameterized arrivals
abstract: Traffic flow modeling is an essential part of civil planning around the world, and traffic simulation is an important component of the analyses that city planners must perform to ensure safe and efficient road networks for their citizens. This work advances microscopic traffic simulation through lane-level validation of speed and flow dynamics, addressing a critical gap in conventional macro-aggregated approaches. We systematically evaluate the trade-offs between numerical integration methods and vehicle arrival processes when reproducing empirical trajectory data from California's freeway network. Results demonstrate that numerical-integrator choice has negligible impact on simulation accuracy, with less than one percent variation across eight methods, while vehicle arrival-process modeling substantially affects fidelity. The shifted Erlang-2 distribution reduces flow-prediction error by approximately 28% compared to Poisson processes by enforcing a realistic minimum headway. Lane-level validation across five detector stations reveals lane-specific dynamics that aggregated metrics often obscure.

title: LAaDT-DSS: decision support for non-experts on rooftop PV, incentive and grid simulations under Turkish tariff rules
abstract: Rooftop photovoltaics raise three questions: should a household invest, which incentive costs the state least, and does the feeder stay within limits? Those who ask are rarely modellers. We present LAaDT-DSS, decision-support software that answers all three under Turkish tariff rules from one simulation core. Non-experts reach it by clicking a house on a 3D map or by asking in plain words; a language model is asked to call the simulation tools, not to compute. Each entry of its 125-entry parameter registry is marked as sourced or estimated. Case studies test the system. Its PV yield lies within $\pm$3.6% of two independent tools at equal losses. Across 2,048 draws of its estimated inputs, the answer for PV alone held in all but one; with a battery, it changed in 31-41% of the draws. Four scripted chat scenarios ran end to end; no user study was run.
